7509.t: Unknown. Ionic word for "lizard" (common being σαύρα (saúra)), perhaps from κρόκη (krókē, “pebble”) + δρῖλος (drîlos, “worm”), because crocodiles like resting on flat stones.

7561.t: Assumed to be from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁- (“to perceive, pay attention”) and therefore related to κοέω (koéō), Latin caveō, Sanskrit कवि (kaví, “wise, poet, seer, sage”), Persian کی (kay, “poet-king”), Lithuanian kavoti (“safeguard, tend”), Old…

7514.t: A Semitic loanword. Compare Akkadian 𒌑𒆪𒄀𒆸𒈾 (/⁠kurkanū⁠/), Arabic كُرْكُم (kurkum), and Hebrew כרכום (karkom).

7535.t: Uncertain. Sometimes considered a Pre-Greek substrate word.

7541.t: A vinicultural loan of Semitic origin, compare Hebrew כַּד (kad), Ugaritic 𐎋𐎄 (kd), Imperial Aramaic 𐡊𐡃 (kd), Punic 𐤊𐤃 (kd).

7532.t: Not related to κύπη (kúpē, “kind of ship”), nor derived from κύπτω (kúptō, “to bend, stoop”). According to Beekes, clearly a Pre-Greek word, given the variant.

7550.t: According to Beekes, from a Proto-Indo-European *ḱerd- (“craft, cunning”) and cognate with Old Irish cerd (“craft, skill”) (< *ḱerd-h₂-), Welsh cerdd (“song”).

7565.t: According to Beekes, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₁g- (“weak, faint”), the same root of λαγαρός (lagarós, “hollow, sunken”), λαγαίω (lagaíō, “to release”), λάγνος (lágnos, “lascivious”), λήγω (lḗgō, “to stop, cease”), and λωγάνιον (lōgánion, “dewlap of…

7520.t: Reminiscent of δοῦπος (doûpos, “thud”), but further details are unknown. The variation between voiced and unvoiced stop suggests Pre-Greek origin.

7560.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kṓpā, from Proto-Indo-European *kóh₂p-eh₂, from the root *keh₂p- (“to seize, grab”), which also gives κάπτω (káptō, “gulp down”).

7549.t: Unknown. Has long been compared to κεράννυμι (keránnumi, “to mix”), but could also be related to Latin cremō, Proto-West Germanic *herþ (English hearth), or Sanskrit कूडयति (kūḍayati, “to burn, scorch”).

7547.t: From the stem of κατόψομαι (katópsomai) (root *h₃ekʷ- (“to see”)), future of καθοράω (kathoráō, “to behold”) + -τρον (-tron, instrument suffix).

7537.t: Probably from a Mediterranean Pre-Greek substrate word, as hinted by the suffixes. Traditionally linked to Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“head, top, skull, horn”).

7546.t: From κάρφω (kárphō, “to dry up, to wither”) + -ος (-os). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐂓 (ka+po).

7582.t: From λείπω (leípō, “to leave, to quit”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).

7553.t: The formation is like other plant names, such as μάνυζα (mánuza), μώλυζα (mṓluza) and ὄρυζα (óruza). The assumption that it was formed from κονίς (konís, “nit”) is unwarranted.

7545.t: The word has been connected with Persian کبر (kabar, “caper”) and Burushaski [script needed] (čopuri) (a language isolate), suggesting an Oriental origin.

7544.t: Uncertain. * The origin of the beetle-name is unclear, but it may be an r-stem-suffixation to κάνθων (kánthōn, “pack-ass”) as suggested by Strömberg, since the scarab is recognized for and likened by his transporting packs of dung.

7516.t: From κεράννυμι (keránnumi, “to mix”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).

7515.t: A similar word for "onion" and "garlic" is found in Proto-West Germanic *hramusō (“onion, garlic”), Proto-Slavic *čermъša (“ramson”) and Middle Irish crem (“wild garlic”), suggesting a derivation from Proto-Indo-European *kermus- (“wild garlic”).

7522.t: Given the unusual formation, according to Beekes, the word is without a doubt Pre-Greek. Frisk and Chantraine discuss it under κυδάζω (kudázō, “to insult”), but the semantic relation seems weak.

7564.t: Unexplained. Connection with Latin lāma (“marsh, mud”) and Lithuanian lōmas (“pit, hollow”) is semantically unconvincing.

7589.t: From λιμός (limós) + κτείνω (kteínō), equivalent to λιμοκτόνος (limoktónos) + -έω (-éō).
